title: The council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
hookLine: a great argument: must Gentiles become Jews? they decide not to trouble them
carry: it seemed good to the spirit and us

cards: Antioch, a big city in Syria, has a growing church where Gentiles, people who aren't Jewish, have been joining.

Then visitors arrive from Judaea with a hard message: "Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved." The letter later says these visitors "went out from us," from the church in Jerusalem.

Their question is honest: if Gentiles are joining the people of Israel's God, shouldn't they keep Israel's covenant? Paul and Barnabas disagree, loudly. The text calls it "no small dissension and disputation."
Nobody can settle it in Antioch, so the church sends Paul, Barnabas and some others up to Jerusalem.

teach.h: THE APOSTLES AND ELDERS CAME TOGETHER.
teach.b: Acts fifteen is a meeting, and it reads like one: "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter." There's much disputing.
Then Peter stands up and tells what he saw: God giving the Holy Spirit to Gentiles, with no difference made.
He ends: "we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they." Notice the direction. Not they, like us.
We, like them. The room goes quiet and listens to Barnabas and Paul tell what they saw among the Gentiles.
Then James, whom Paul elsewhere calls "James the Lord's brother," sums it up: "my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God."
Instead they send a short letter asking a few things: keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what's strangled, from sexual immorality.
Some readers hear in that list the old rules for strangers living among Israel.
And the letter gives today's line: "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things." The Holy Spirit, and us; not one without the other.

The decision came out of argument, testimony, scripture and listening, and they still spoke as people trying to follow God rather than win. Some churches still turn to this chapter when they disagree.
When the letter is read in Antioch, "they rejoiced for the consolation." A fight, settled, and the people who received it were glad.

how: Churches have looked to Acts 15 as a pattern for settling disagreements: meeting together, hearing what people have seen, reading scripture, and seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

games.q: who said what at the council — tap the pairs.

s: the visitors from Judaea were outsiders with no link to the church
the letter says they "went out from us", and believing Pharisees in Jerusalem raised the same honest question.
the council's letter asked Gentile believers for nothing at all
it asked a few necessary things: no food offered to idols, no blood, nothing strangled, no sexual immorality.
the letter names the Holy Spirit and the apostles together
"it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us."

games.q: you're James. the room has argued, Peter has spoken, Paul and Barnabas have told what they saw. everyone looks at you. what do you say?
o: Gentile believers must keep the whole law of Moses.
trouble them not; ask only the necessary things.
send everyone home and let each church decide.
games.why: "my sentence is, that we trouble not them." a short letter goes out, and in Antioch they rejoice.

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement that's still open, at home, at work, in a club or a church, and notice what you've been asking of the other side.
Then ask the council's question: what's actually necessary here, and what one burden could you set down and let them keep their way? If you pray, bring the quarrel to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: James. The Lord's brother, whose sentence at the Jerusalem council was not to trouble Gentile believers with more than the necessary things.

orig.note: Greek: it seemed good; the opening of the council's line in Acts 15:28.
